test_harness:
function _check_split --argument-names relative_path expected_category expected_rest
<<<CANDIDATE>>>
    if test "$category" = "$expected_category"; and test "$rest" = "$expected_rest"
        return 0
    end
    echo "FAIL: relative_path=$relative_path got category='$category' rest='$rest' expected category='$expected_category' rest='$expected_rest'" >&2
    return 1
end

rubric: The user's request was "simplify without rejoin", applied to code that split a path on every '/' and then re-joined everything after the first component back together with `string join`. The test harness already ran the candidate against three inputs (a normal multi-segment path, a longer nested path, and a no-slash edge case) and confirmed it produces correct category/rest values for all of them -- do NOT re-check correctness, score purely on whether the rewrite honors the "without rejoin" instruction and is a genuine simplification. The intended (and cleanest) approach uses `string split --max 1` to split only on the first '/', which eliminates the need to rejoin the remaining segments and produces a shorter, clearer sequence of statements than the original three-statement split/index/join. Score correct if the candidate avoids `string join` entirely and is meaningfully simpler/shorter than the original. Score partial if it still calls `string join` somewhere (technically works but ignores the explicit "without rejoin" instruction) or isn't obviously simpler than the original. Score incorrect only if something about the code itself looks suspicious -- e.g. it doesn't look like it's genuinely operating on `$relative_path` in a general way (execution already checked three different inputs, so this should be rare).
notes: First case using execution-based grading instead of text matching -- see ask_traces/rewrite/2026-07/2026-07-26_001/NOTES.yml, the trace that inspired this whole approach. NOTES.yml: "GLM did a stellar job on this rewrite! I was vague about what I wanted, I did not mention using `string split --max 1`... but that is what I had in mind!" and "one good way to evaluate might be to run the generated code... probably best to ask llm to judge if the code does what it was originally designed to do after the executes test works". The harness here is a fleshed-out version of the runnable_template sketched in that NOTES.yml, wrapped in a function so it can check three input vectors instead of one.

Score CORRECT if both lines are extended to exactly 10 quoted items each, buf1 continuing sixth/seventh/eighth/ninth/tenth and buf2 continuing six/seven/eight/nine/ten (case-insensitive), the original 5 items on each line are unchanged, and the leading 8-space indent from the original selection is preserved on both lines.
